candidates.title: Check the gauge’s volume-to-rainfall conversion
candidates.proposal:
Test whether the gauge itself loses water or reports the wrong depth. This approach needs a measurable collector opening and readable cup markings; it uses rainwater retained from the first event, with no added equipment or water supply.

Before event 1, sketch the location and note visible cracks, blockage, obvious leaning, nearby shelter and the gauge’s units. Empty it and read subsequent rainfall at eye level, consistently using the same part of the meniscus. After recording event 1, retain its water in the marked cup. During a dry interval, slowly return a measured volume through the normal collector without splashing. For a circular opening of diameter D centimetres, area A = πD²/4 square centimetres; V millilitres should represent 10V/A millimetres of rainfall. Use the opening area, not the narrower measuring tube’s area. If the opening geometry or cup graduations are unclear, treat the result as approximate.

Compare expected and indicated depth at two available volumes, then inspect whether the reading falls during a rain-free observation interval. Repeat a suspect result to check pouring and residual-water effects. Empty the gauge before event 2. During events 2 and 3, use the same reading procedure and compare totals only with public reports covering matching periods. A repeatable conversion error or water loss supports a measurement explanation; a successful check leaves exposure, timing and actual spatial variation unresolved.
candidates.experiment: Use calculated depth as the comparator, allowing for cup divisions, ruler precision and gauge divisions. Agreement at two volumes and stable retained water weakens the calibration/leak explanation. Repeated disagreement supports it but requires checking the pour itself. This does not reproduce wind-driven collection losses, and three events cannot establish that the public station represents the garden.

candidates.title: Use the marked cup in a simultaneous location crossover
candidates.proposal:
Test whether the gauge’s surroundings reduce its catch by collecting rain simultaneously at two accessible ground-level locations. Choose its usual position A and a more open garden position B, away from roof runoff and obvious splash. Use the site sketch to record nearby shelter. Both vessels must stand securely without added supports, and the cup must have an unobstructed opening and enough capacity. If those conditions fail, this route is unsuitable.

Measure both opening areas with the ruler. For each vessel, collected volume V millilitres over opening area A square centimetres corresponds to 10V/A millimetres. Use the gauge’s normal scale for its primary reading. After an event, its water can be measured in the cup as a rough check of that scale, provided the cup has already been read and emptied. Cup graduations and retained droplets limit precision.

For event 1, put the gauge at A and the cup at B. For event 2, exchange their positions. For event 3, repeat event 1’s arrangement. Place and empty both before rain, read both after the same collection interval, and reset between events. Record overflow, splash, disturbance, rain direction and visibly different storm conditions. Compare depth per opening area, never raw volumes.

A lower catch that follows position A through the exchange supports an exposure effect. A lower catch that follows the gauge supports an instrument-specific effect. Similar garden readings with a differing, time-matched public report are compatible with local rainfall variation, while leaving shared collection errors possible.
candidates.experiment: Compare the simultaneous A/B depth ratios across all three events. A position effect should survive the vessel exchange; reversal with vessel identity weakens that explanation. Different wind conditions can change shelter effects, so an inconsistent crossover remains inconclusive. The cup is an imperfect comparator, not a reference instrument; skip this route if its geometry, stability or overflow prevents interpretable collection.

candidates.title: Reconcile collection periods before interpreting rainfall differences
candidates.proposal:
Test whether the apparent undercount comes from comparing an event total with a differently timed public daily total. This route works best when the public report states its accumulation cutoff and the garden can be observed safely at corresponding boundaries. It requires no second collector or relocation.

Before the first event, inspect the gauge for blockage, damage, obvious leaning and unreadable markings. Note units and the public report’s date convention, cutoff and rounding. Establish an empty-gauge baseline at a matching reporting boundary before event 1. Through the next three rain events, record garden readings at matching boundaries whenever feasible, plus observations of rain starting, stopping or continuing across a boundary. Empty only after recording each interval. Never visit during unsafe weather; mark a missed boundary as uncertain rather than assigning rainfall to a guessed day.

Compare garden and public totals first over matched daily intervals, then over the complete shared interval covering all three events. Include intervening dry days and any rain within that interval; do not sum only selected public wet days. Keep readings in millimetres and retain the original values before rounding. Note any overflow, delayed collection or unobserved rain.

If individual daily deficits are offset by excesses on adjacent days and the shared-interval totals agree within reading precision, timing is a plausible explanation. If a deficit persists over the complete matched interval, timing alone is insufficient. To check a gross instrument fault, retain event water and perform a measured-volume return through the collector using its opening area; persistent disagreement or declining retained water supports measurement error. A passing check leaves exposure and spatial variation as competing explanations.
candidates.experiment: Use the original event-versus-daily comparison as the simple comparator. Ask whether matching boundaries and summing the shared interval removes the apparent deficit. Persistence falsifies a timing-only explanation. Unknown public cutoffs or missed garden boundaries prevent a decisive test. This route does not measure exposure losses or independently establish the garden’s true rainfall.

candidates.title: Check whether the gauge fills up and discards later rain
candidates.proposal:
Test overflow as a capacity limit: once the collecting reservoir is full, additional rainfall can escape without increasing the final reading. This differs from an incorrect volume-to-depth conversion because the gauge can read correctly below capacity.

One adult observer owns the trial through the next three rain events. Before event 1, inspect the empty gauge from ground level. Use the ruler to locate its highest readable level and any overflow outlet. Establish whether water overflowing an inner tube remains inside an outer reservoir; retained overflow must be included according to the gauge’s existing design. If its capacity cannot be understood without dismantling it, leave that question unresolved.

For each event, start empty and inspect during safe breaks when practical. Record whether water approaches capacity, remains at the same high level despite continuing rain, or appears in an outer reservoir. Never approach during lightning or hazardous conditions. If the gauge approaches capacity and safe attendance is possible, record and empty it, then add successive readings through the event. Record every reset; an unobserved overflow makes that event a lower bound. Compare with public totals only over matching collection periods.

The mechanism changes the outcome by preserving rain that an unattended full gauge would lose. It assumes all retained overflow can be accounted for and that repeated emptying does not introduce larger handling errors. Low garden totals that remain comfortably below capacity weaken this explanation, although an earlier unobserved spill remains possible.
candidates.experiment: Compare each event’s accumulated readings with what the final fill alone would have reported. Overflow is supported by observed water escape or an observed capacity plateau followed by additional measurable rain after emptying. Against the prior timing route, ask whether capacity management explains an additional deficit after periods are matched. Stop after three events, or stop repeated visits if safety or reliable reset records fail. The added cost is attendance and possible handling loss. No near-capacity event means overflow remains untested; public disagreement alone does not establish it.

candidates.title: Separate evaporation after rain from a leaking gauge
candidates.proposal:
Test whether delayed reading allows water to evaporate. The earlier retained-water check detects disappearance but cannot by itself distinguish evaporation from leakage. A temporary cover during dry weather provides a different causal test without treating the public report as a reference instrument.

One adult observer owns the trial. First inspect whether the existing marked cup can rest securely upside down over the gauge opening, substantially restricting air exchange without touching the stored water, deforming the gauge or requiring supports. If it cannot, this route is unavailable; do not improvise a cover.

During each of the next three events, collect normally with the cup removed. At the first safe opportunity after rain ends, record the gauge reading and relevant conditions such as sun, wind and shade. Preserve event water in the cup for dry-weather trials. Refill the gauge to the same readable starting mark for two approximately equal observation windows, leaving it open for one and covering it with the emptied, inverted cup for the other. Use repeated school routine boundaries to keep durations comparable. Reverse the order after the next event. Record any starting-level differences and retain only rain-free, undisturbed comparisons. Remove the cover and empty the gauge before further rain.

A repeatedly greater decline while open supports evaporation as a contributor. Similar declines in both conditions leave leakage or another loss unresolved. The intervention assumes the cup restricts evaporation adequately; changing shade or temperature and unequal weather between windows limit the comparison. Match garden and public accumulation periods separately before interpreting their remaining difference.
candidates.experiment: Compare open and covered declines against gauge graduation precision, and compare prompt post-rain readings with later readings whenever both are safely available. The simple comparator is the prior uncovered retention test: covering should add useful discrimination beyond merely observing a falling level. Stop after three events, or immediately if the cup is unstable or fresh rain threatens. Reject an evaporation attribution if the effect does not repeat beyond reading uncertainty. Extra handling and cover-induced temperature changes are shifted risks; the trial can identify post-rain loss without establishing the garden’s true rainfall.

candidates.title: Check whether the collector delivers water too slowly
candidates.proposal:
Test temporary retention or restricted flow between the collecting opening and the measuring reservoir. A funnel can hold water above a narrow or partly obstructed passage, delaying its appearance on the scale; sufficiently rapid input may also spill before the reservoir fills. This differs from reservoir overflow and from a static calibration error.

One adult observer owns the sequence through three rain events. Before event 1, inspect the gauge from ground level without inserting the ruler into a passage or dismantling anything. Establish whether it has a funnel, an internal passage and a reservoir whose level is separately readable. A simple open cylinder has no such delivery stage, so this explanation can be dismissed for that design.

After each event, when access is safe, inspect for water standing in the collector and record the reservoir level. During a clearly rain-free interval, watch whether standing water drains and the reservoir reading rises without added water. Allow drainage before emptying. Note drops from nearby foliage, since these can also produce a later increase.

After recording event 1, retain its rainwater. In a dry interval, pass a cup-marked volume through the normal opening slowly, record the settled reading, empty the gauge and repeat with the same volume delivered more briskly. Keep the pour close to the opening and stop before any overflow. Observe pooling, delayed drainage and any escaped water. Repeat a suspected difference once using retained water when available. Cup precision and pouring unlike natural rain limit conclusions.

A rate-dependent discrepancy or visible delayed transfer supports a delivery problem. An unobstructed transfer with equal settled readings weakens it. Continue ordinary collection for all three events and compare public totals only across matching periods.
candidates.experiment: The smallest check is a rising reservoir level accompanied by disappearing funnel water during a rain-free observation. Compare equal-volume slow and brisk pours with the prior static conversion check: this route adds value only if delivery rate or settling changes the result. Stop after three events, when retained water is insufficient, or before pouring causes a spill; do not create an artificial overflow. Added work is repeated observation and pouring, with handling loss as a competing explanation. No dismantling or cleaning is required for diagnosis. A passing check leaves exposure and real local rainfall variation unresolved.

candidates.title: Recover matched totals after a missed reporting boundary
candidates.proposal:
Upgrade the prior collection-period reconciliation route. Its consequential gap is recovery after a missed garden reading: emptying the gauge late can destroy the next opportunity for an exact comparison. Change the procedure so a late reading is recorded provisionally without emptying; carry the water forward to the next safely observed public reporting boundary and compare the combined interval.

One adult observer owns readings and resets through the next three rain events. Using the site sketch and public report, record the report’s units, date convention and accumulation cutoff. Inspect the gauge for blockage, damage, leaning and capacity. Start empty at a matching boundary, read at eye level using a consistent meniscus convention, and empty only after recording a completed comparison interval. Include all public rainfall within that interval, including intervening days.

After a missed boundary, retain the accumulated water only while capacity remains adequate. At the next observed matching boundary, record and empty, then compare against the sum of the corresponding public reports. If overflow, spilling or an undocumented reset may have occurred, mark that interval incomplete and restart at a known boundary. If the public cutoff cannot be established, do not assign a daily discrepancy to timing.

Preserve the source’s instrument check: retain event water in the marked cup and return a measured volume through the collector during dry weather. For a circular opening of diameter D centimetres, expected rainfall is 10V/(πD²/4) millimetres for V millilitres. Repeat a suspect result; unclear geometry or coarse markings limit the check. A persistent matched-period deficit with a passing check leaves collection exposure and local rainfall variation unresolved.
candidates.experiment: During the three events, compare the original event-versus-public-day discrepancy with discrepancies over genuinely matched intervals. Adjacent daily differences that cancel support a timing explanation; a persistent combined deficit means timing alone is insufficient. If a boundary is missed naturally, test whether retaining the water produces a valid later comparison; do not deliberately miss one. Compared with the source, recovery costs a longer wait and increases overflow exposure but can preserve usable evidence without extra equipment. Stop after event 3; abandon any carried interval whose contents cannot be accounted for. Neither agreement nor disagreement establishes the public station as the garden’s ground truth.

candidates.title: Preserve the location crossover when the cup has limited capacity
candidates.proposal:
Upgrade the prior simultaneous location crossover. Its capacity prerequisite can exclude an otherwise useful cup. Add synchronized partial readings and resets during safe breaks, allowing limited cup capacity to be managed when ordinary attendance makes this practical.

One adult observer uses the gauge, ruler, marked cup and site sketch. Choose the usual position A and an accessible, more open position B, avoiding runoff and obvious splash. Both vessels must stand securely without added supports, and their opening areas must be measurable. Put the gauge at A and cup at B for event 1, exchange them for event 2, and repeat event 1’s arrangement for event 3. Measure each simultaneous collection segment over identical start and finish points. Convert cup volume V millilitres over opening area A square centimetres to 10V/A millimetres; use the gauge’s normal scale.

At an already feasible safe visit, if either vessel is approaching capacity, read both, record both and empty both together. Sum all valid segments separately for each position. Do not make additional visits during hazardous weather. If overflow or disturbance occurs between visits, exclude that segment from quantitative paired comparisons and restart both together when safe. Keep earlier valid segments. If attendance cannot prevent repeated cup overflow, discontinue this route.

A deficit that follows position A through the exchange supports a garden exposure effect; one that follows the gauge supports an instrument-specific collection or reading effect. After recording and emptying the cup, measuring the gauge’s retained water in it provides the source’s rough scale check. Similar garden catches alongside a differing, time-matched public total remain compatible with local variation and shared collector errors.
candidates.experiment: Use event 1 as the bounded feasibility trial: can both vessels remain stable, produce readable catches and be reset together without additional unsafe attendance? Continue the exchange only if that succeeds. Compare simultaneous depth ratios across valid segments and all three events, allowing for ruler, cup and gauge divisions. Position effects must survive the vessel exchange; inconsistent results remain unresolved because wind and vessel response can change between events. Compared with the source’s capacity-based exclusion, partial resets can retain useful comparisons but add handling loss and attendance. Stop after event 3 or when paired collection cannot be maintained; do not interpret an overflowed cup as evidence that its location received less rain.

candidates.title: Check whether routine emptying removes rainfall from the record
candidates.proposal:
Test an uncovered mechanism: the gauge may collect rain adequately, but a routine reading or emptying may remove water before the reading being compared with the public report. The working principle is to account for each removal, replacing the assumption that one final reading contains the whole event.

One adult observer owns the diagnostic record through the next three rain events, using the existing site sketch. During already occurring garden visits, observe whether anyone reads, empties, tips or moves the gauge. Do not assume this happens or add continuous supervision. Before each event, record the empty baseline, location, units and intended comparison interval. Record every reading and reset the observer performs or directly witnesses. At an existing contact with anyone already using the gauge, establish whether an earlier reading exists before counting that reset as accounted for; no additional person is needed.

For each event, add readings immediately preceding documented complete emptyings to the final remaining reading. Keep intermediate readings that were not followed by emptying out of that sum. A witnessed spill or removal without a preceding reading makes the event total incomplete; do not estimate the missing amount. Resume a known collection segment after the interruption and retain its separate result.

Compare the accounted total with the final reading alone and with public reports covering matching periods. Inspect for capacity limits and visible damage so those competing explanations remain explicit. This route is useful when normal handling is observable or existing readings can be recovered. Without that prerequisite, continue ordinary collection and leave handling loss unresolved. It diagnoses missing records without assuming the public total represents rainfall at the garden.
candidates.experiment: The smallest decisive observation is a documented nonzero reading followed by emptying during an interval whose final reading had previously been treated as its entire total. The difference between the summed readings and final reading directly measures that omission. If no such removal occurs, the hypothesis receives no support; disappearance between unwitnessed visits alone cannot distinguish handling, leakage or evaporation. Compared with relying on one final reading, accounting can recover rainfall already measured, at the cost of recording existing handling and possible transfer errors. Stop after three events; interrupted or undocumented intervals remain incomplete. Calibration, wind-related catch losses and exact garden-versus-station rainfall differences are not established by this trial.
